JLPT N5 to N1: Skills, Test Times and Scores Compared (2026)

Kanjidon Team · Jan 30, 2026

The five JLPT levels run from N5, the entry level, to N1, the highest. The official differences are expressed as receptive language abilities, test structure and score thresholds—not as fixed kanji totals, study hours, job titles or fluency labels. This comparison uses the current 2026 timings and official pass marks.

Official Level Comparison

LevelCondensed official ability summaryTotal test timeOverall pass mark
N5Understand some basic Japanese90 minutes80/180
N4Understand basic Japanese115 minutes90/180
N3Understand everyday Japanese to a certain degree140 minutes95/180
N2Understand everyday Japanese and Japanese used in wider circumstances to a certain degree155 minutes90/180
N1Understand Japanese used in a variety of circumstances165 minutes100/180

Total times are the sum of the official timed test sections: N5 20+40+30, N4 25+55+35, N3 30+70+40, N2 105+50 and N1 110+55 minutes. Venue administration and breaks can make the full visit longer.

Sectional Minimums Also Decide the Result

LevelsScoring sectionsMinimum in each
N1, N2, N3Language Knowledge; Reading; Listening (0–60 each)19/60 in every section
N4, N5Language Knowledge and Reading (0–120); Listening (0–60)38/120 and 19/60

A candidate must meet the overall pass mark and every sectional minimum and must take all required sections. Official results are scaled; they are not obtained by assigning one point to every correct item.

N5 and N4: Basic Japanese

N5 asks whether you can understand some basic written expressions and short, slowly spoken conversations. N4 expands that foundation to basic passages and everyday conversations spoken slowly. Neither level has an official kanji count, and neither should be described as a guarantee that travel will be effortless.

N3: The Bridge Level

N3 was designed as a bridge between N4/N5 and N1/N2. The official summary includes reading everyday materials with specific contents and understanding headlines, plus generally following coherent everyday conversations at near-natural speed. “To a certain degree” matters: the certificate is not a blanket claim about every real-world situation.

N2: A Wider Range of Circumstances

N2 includes reading articles and commentaries on general topics and following coherent conversations and news reports at nearly natural speed. It is often requested by institutions, but the JLPT does not promise employment, admission or a visa. Check the organisation that matters to you.

N1: Advanced Receptive Understanding

N1 covers logically complex or abstract writing and natural-speed spoken material across varied circumstances. It remains a selected-response test of language knowledge, reading and listening. It does not directly measure conversation, pronunciation, handwriting or professional translation.

How to Choose a Level

  • Read the official ability summary, not a third-party fluency label.
  • Try fresh official sample questions without a dictionary.
  • Check whether you can finish within the current time for that level.
  • Look for a target slightly above your current reliable performance, not several levels above an app streak.
  • If an employer, school or immigration route is the reason, confirm its exact current requirement directly.
